The Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra) – Analysis 10
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāravibhaṅga). Therein, what is the mode of conveying synonyms?
It is: "There are many synonyms."
Just as the Blessed One explains a single state of phenomena by means of various synonyms.
As the Blessed One said:
"Hope, longing, and delight..."
“Desires are established in many elements;
they arise from the root of ignorance and are pursued through longing.
All of them, together with their roots, have been brought to an end by me.”
"Hope" (āsā) is said to be the longing for a future object, thinking "it will certainly come to pass," whereby hope arises.
"Longing" (pihā) is the aspiration for a present object; or, having seen something better, longing arises with the thought, "May I become like this.
"Delight" (abhinandanā) is the preservation of the accomplishment of an object; one delights in a dear relative, or one delights in a dear teaching, or one delights because it is not disagreeable.
"Many elements" means: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the flavor element, and the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Sarāti: some are intent on forms, some on sounds, some on odors, some on tastes, some on tangibles, and some on mental phenomena.
Therein, the six types of worldly displeasure, the six types of worldly joy, the six types of renunciate displeasure, and the six types of renunciate joy—these are the twenty-four factors.
The side of craving; this is a synonym for craving.
Those six kinds of equanimity based on the household life are the side of views.
That same [equanimity], when it takes the form of aspiration, is delight in phenomena, love of phenomena, and attachment to phenomena—this is a synonym for craving.
“Citta,” “mano,” and “viññāṇa” are synonyms for consciousness (citta).
“Manindriya,” “manodhātu,” “manāyatana,” and “vijānana” are synonyms for the mind (mano).
“Paññindriya,” “paññābala,” “adhipaññā,” “sikkhā,” “paññā,” “paññākkhandha,” and “dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga” [are synonyms for wisdom].
Knowledge, right view, investigation, insight, knowledge of phenomena, knowledge of meaning, knowledge of sequence,
knowledge of destruction, knowledge of non-arising, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing,
the faculty of one who has known, vision, clear knowledge, intelligence, vast wisdom, sagacity, light— whatever else is of this same nature, these are synonyms for wisdom.
The five faculties pertaining to the supramundane are all wisdom.

Moreover, in the sense of predominance, there is faith; in the sense of exertion, energy; in the sense of non-forgetfulness, mindfulness; in the sense of non-distraction, concentration; and in the sense of understanding, wisdom.

And as it is said in the Recollection of the Buddha: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
He has attained mastery over the powers, reached intrepidity, acquired the analytical knowledges, abandoned the four yokes, transcended the paths of wrong going;
he has extracted the thorn, healed the wound, crushed the bramble, extinguished the obsessions, gone beyond bonds, untied the knots, transcended underlying tendencies,
shattered the darkness, possesses vision, transcended worldly conditions, and is free from attachment and aversion.
Regarding agreeable and disagreeable phenomena, they have reached the unreckonable, transcended bondage, and withdrawn from battle;

they are more excellent, bearers of torches, makers of light, makers of radiance, dispellers of darkness, abandoners of strife, possessed of immeasurable beauty, unfathomable beauty, and incalculable beauty;
they are makers of splendor, makers of brilliance, and illuminators of the radiance of Dhamma—such indeed are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
And this is a synonym for the recollection of the Buddha.

And as it was said regarding the recollection of the Dhamma: "The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One—visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized individually by the wise.

That is to say: the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle of existence, the void, exceedingly difficult to attain, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna."
“The unconditioned, infinite, and taintless,
the truth, the further shore, subtle and very hard to see;
ageless, stable, and clearly perceived— ”
Non-manifest, free from proliferation,
peaceful, deathless, sublime, auspicious, secure,
the destruction of craving— wonderful and marvelous.
Free from affliction, having the nature of being free from affliction—
this is Nibbāna, taught by the Sugata;
it is unborn, unbecome, and free from calamity.
The uncreated, sorrowless, and free from grief;
free from affliction and beyond the nature of affliction—
this is Nibbāna, taught by the Sugata.
Profound and difficult to see,
supreme and unsurpassed,
peerless and without equal.
It is called the eldest and the best;
it is called a shelter, a refuge, free from conflict, stainless, without blemish, and pure.
"The island, the immeasurable happiness, the foundation,
the state of nothingness, and the absence of conceptual proliferation"—
this is a synonym for the recollection of the Dhamma.
And as it is said in the Recollection of the Saṅgha: "Well-practiced, uprightly practiced, practicing the way, practicing with propriety— namely,
the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals— this is the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality,
worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world, endowed with virtue."
"Endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation;
the essence of beings, the cream of beings, the rescue of beings, the pillar of beings, the fragrant flower among beings—
one who is worthy of honor by both gods and humans"— this is a synonym for the recollection of the Saṅgha.

And as it was said in the *Sīlānussati*: "Those virtues which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, noble, praised by the noble ones, liberating, commended by the wise, unattached to, and conducive to concentration;
virtue is an ornament because of its excellence in adorning the highest limb; and virtue is a treasure-store in the sense of transcending all wretchedness."
Virtue is a craft in the sense of hitting the mark; virtue is a time in the sense of not transgressing the proper occasion;
virtue is grain in the sense of ending poverty; virtue is a mirror in the sense of reflecting the Dhamma; virtue is a palace in the sense of providing a view;
and virtue is that which accompanies one through all planes, having the Deathless as its consummation—this is a synonym for the recollection of virtue.

And just as it was stated in the *Recollection of Generosity* (*cāgānussati*)—“At whatever time a noble disciple dwells at home, he is one who is open-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to giving, and fond of sharing”—this is a synonym for the recollection of generosity.
Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: “The synonyms are many.
Thus concludes the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (*vevacanahāra*).
